events.title: Pedro de Alvarado conquers the Maya of Guatemala and Cuzcatlán
events.place: Guatemalan Highlands and western El Salvador
events.summary: Sent by Hernán Cortés, Pedro de Alvarado invaded the Maya kingdoms of Guatemala in 1524, burned the Kʼicheʼ kings alive and their capital Qʼumarkaj, and campaigned against the Pipil of Cuzcatlán in present-day El Salvador until 1528.
account: Cortés despatched Pedro de Alvarado with 180 cavalry, 300 infantry, crossbows, muskets, 4 cannons and thousands of allied warriors from Tlaxcala, Cholula and other cities of central Mexico; they arrived in Soconusco in 1523. A Kʼicheʼ army was defeated in the Quetzaltenango valley in February 1524 and many Kʼicheʼ nobles were among the dead; local tradition places the death of the prince Tecun Uman in these battles.

In March 1524 Alvarado entered Qʼumarkaj, the Kʼicheʼ capital, at the invitation of its remaining lords. He seized the king Oxib-Keh and the king-elect Beleheb-Tzy in his camp, had the captured lords burnt to death, and then burned the entire city. He then demanded gold in tribute from the Kaqchikel, and by 1526 rebellions had engulfed the highlands. Bartolomé de las Casas charged him with further atrocities in the conquest of the Maya kingdoms.

The same year Alvarado led an expedition against the Pipil province of Cuzcatlán but retreated to Guatemala by July 1524. San Salvador, founded in 1525, was destroyed in a native rising in 1526; Alvarado campaigned again in 1526 and 1528, and the uprising ended in 1528 when the Spanish stormed the native stronghold at the Peñol de Cinacantan. The conquest of Guatemala's other peoples went on until the Petén fell in 1697. Disease, chiefly smallpox and measles, is counted at 1,600,000 dead between 1525 and 1550, and an estimated 33–50% of the highland population perished.

events.title: The Mixtón War
events.summary: In 1540–1542 the Caxcanes and their allies rose to drive the Spanish out of northwestern Mexico, after a decade in which Nuño de Guzmán had killed, tortured and enslaved thousands; Pedro de Alvarado died in the war, and Viceroy Mendoza crushed the revolt.

Over six years he killed, tortured and enslaved thousands of natives; his policy was to "terrorize the natives with often unprovoked killing, torture, and enslavement", and the Spanish tried to force the natives into servitude through the encomienda.

In spring 1540 the Caxcanes struck back. The spark was apparently the arrest of eighteen native leaders and the hanging of nine of them; many fled the encomiendas to the hill fortress of Mixtón in Zacatecas. Led by Francisco Tenamaztle, the rising was put down by Viceroy Antonio de Mendoza with Tlaxcalan and Mexica allies by 1542; Pedro de Alvarado was killed in the campaign.

events.title: The cocoliztli epidemics of 1545 and 1576
events.summary: Waves of a hemorrhagic fever the Aztecs called cocoliztli, 'pestilence', killed an estimated 5 to 15 million people in sixteenth-century New Spain; it fell most heavily on the Indigenous people.
account: The cocoliztli epidemic, an illness of high fevers and bleeding, caused 5–15 million deaths in New Spain during the 16th century and is often called the worst epidemic in Mexico's history. Its largest outbreaks were in 1545 and 1576; a second large outbreak in 1576 lasted until about 1580 and caused approximately two million deaths. Spanish accounts cite 13 cocoliztli epidemics between 1545 and 1642.

Researchers disagree on the cause: genomic studies point to Salmonella enterica Paratyphi C, while others propose an Indigenous viral hemorrhagic fever worsened by drought and by the poor living conditions of the Indigenous peoples after the conquest. The encomendero Gonzalo de Ortiz wrote that God sent such sickness on the Indians that three out of every four perished; the modern consensus is that Indigenous people were the most affected.
